In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a storm-dominated, nearshore environment is not in a steady state, but rather in a dynamic state of equilibrium.
the mean flow is not a good indicator of sediment transport in this storm-dominated, barred system, while the low-order moments (and in particular the skewness) are.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a steady-state sediment prism over the storm cycle can be maintained in the presence of a storm-induced offshore mean flow if the net transport vector can be shown to be onshore.

the nearshore is a dynamic and highly complex system, with a wide variety of physical processes operating over a wide range of scales and that these processes can be understood and predicted only by considering the full range of temporal and spatial scales.
the mean velocity field is not a reliable indicator of net sediment flux, even in the absence of significant wave asymmetry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mean velocity field is not sufficient to explain the sediment transport and equilibrium slope in a storm-dominated nearshore system.

, in order to understand the dynamics of a nearshore system, it is not sufficient to consider the mean flow, but that the full velocity distribution must be considered, and the instantaneous transport vector must be calculated.

, for a storm-dominated, two-barred shoreface, the low-order moments (i.e. mean, variance and skewness) of the near-bed, horizontal velocity field can be used to infer the net water and sediment transport, and the bedform migration, but only when the instantaneous transport vector is considered.
